## Overview

The Newar are a distinct linguistic and cultural group primarily inhabiting the Kathmandu Valley and surrounding areas of Nepal. They are the creators of much of the valley’s historic heritage and civilisation, and their community includes diverse ethnic, caste and religious strands. Newars numbered 1,341,363 people in the 2021 Nepal census, constituting 4.6% of Nepal’s population. Their common language, Nepal Bhasa, belongs to the Tibeto-Burman branch of the Sino-Tibetan language family. Newars predominantly practise Newar Hinduism and Newar Buddhism. Their cultural importance is expressed through urban civilisation, hereditary occupations, religious art, architecture, music, dance, festivals, literature, trade, agriculture and cuisine.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Motif vocabulary.** Religious motifs, ritual objects, mythical beasts and birds are named in descriptions of Newar architectural carving, but no textile motifs are documented.

### Architecture

Newar architecture developed in the Kathmandu Valley and surrounding Nepal Mandala. Its structures include pagodas, shikhara, stupas, chaityas, temples, priest houses, palaces, rest houses, residential houses, monastic courtyards known as *bahal* and *bahil*, sacred houses, open-air shrines, dance platforms, sunken water fountains, bazaars and compact streets. Fine brickwork and woodcarving are characteristic. Bare brick walls carry artistic windows and doors, while carved windows, temple roof struts and temple or shrine-house tympana display religious motifs, ritual objects, mythical beasts and birds. The chief monuments are concentrated in the Durbar Squares of Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur. The multiple-roofed pagoda is described as the valley’s trademark. Desay Madu Jhya is identified as a specimen of Newar woodcarving, while the Peacock Window of Bhaktapur and Desay Madu Jhya of Kathmandu are noted for their carved wood.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Newar artistry includes copper and brass sculptures, stone sculpture, wood carving, repoussé art and metal statues of Buddhist and Hindu deities made by lost-wax casting. Newar artisans also worked as potters, clay workers, coppersmiths, bronzesmiths, architects and carpenters. The sources name Kumhā/Prajapati as potterers and clay workers, Tamrakar as a group traditionally involved as coppersmiths, and Kansakar as bronzesmiths. Food and drink are cooked, stored and served in vessels made from gold, silver, copper, brass, iron, clay pottery, dried rice stalks, corn leaves and sewn leaves. Named utensils include *anti*, an alcohol jar; *bātā*, a basin; *chupi*, a knife; *dhampo*, a water pot; *hāsā*, a round winnowing tray; *karuwā*, a water jug; *kholā*, a bowl; *sali*, a small clay bowl; and *somā*, an earthen wine pitcher.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They do identify Newars as jewelry makers and describe Shakya as traditionally including goldsmiths.

## Music & performance

Traditional Newar music consists of sacred music, devotional songs, seasonal songs, ballads and folk songs. Newa music developed in Nepal among the Newars and has roots in classical Hindu and Buddhist music, incorporating folk music from the Kathmandu Valley and its peripheries. Traditional songs include hymns describing deities, songs about love and marriage, ballads, rice-transplantation songs and historical narratives. Traditional musicians worship Nasah Dyah, the Newar god of music and dance.

One important form is **Dapha music**, classical Newar music associated with bands known as *Dapha Khalah*, which may be connected with traditional groups called *Guthi*. Its devotional songs are based on classical ragas, and particular songs are performed at specific seasons or times of day. Music also accompanies religious processions, wedding processions, life-cycle ceremonies and funeral processions. *Bhajan* are devotional songs sung daily in community houses, while *Dapha* songs are sung during hymn-singing seasons in temple squares and sacred courtyards. *Gunla Bajan* bands parade through the streets during Gunla, the 10th month of the Nepal Sambat calendar.

Named percussion instruments include *dhimay*, *khin*, *naykhin*, *dhaa*, *paschima*, *kwonchakhin*, *damakhin*, *dholak*, *nagara* and *kantan dab dab*. Wind instruments include *bansuri*, *mwahali*, *ponga* and *kaahan*. Other instruments include the string instruments *piwancha* and *sarangi*, and idiophones such as *taa*, *babhu*, *chhusyaa*, *kaynpin* and *bhusyaa*. Seturam Shrestha made the first recording of *Rajamati* on gramophone disc in Kolkata in 1908.

## Dance & theatre

Newar dance includes sacred masked dance, religious dance without masks known as *Dyah Pyakhan*, ritual and meditation dance known as *Chachaa Pyakhan*, and folk dance. *Chachaa Pyakhan* is also known as *Charya Nritya* in Sanskrit. Masked dance dramas called *Daboo Pyakhan* enact religious stories with musical accompaniment. The dance performed to the tune of *dhime* is called *Dhime dance*.

Newar music also accompanied traditional epics and plays written in Sanskrit and Nepal Bhasa. The sources describe a raga and taal system and identify manuscripts concerned with dance, drama and stage play, including *Sangit Chandra Grantha*, written by King Jagatjyoti Malla of Bhaktapur and his minister Vanshamani Ojha, and *Gayanlochan*, written by King Jitamitra Malla.

## Festivals & rituals

Newar religious culture is marked by frequent festivals throughout the year. Festivals are connected with Hindu and Buddhist holidays and the harvest cycle, and celebrations follow the lunar calendar, so their dates are changeable. Street celebrations include pageants, *jatras* and processions in which a car or portable shrine is carried through the streets. Other festivals involve family feasts, worship and sacred masked dances.

*Mohani* is an annual celebration lasting several days and involving feasts, religious services and processions. During *Swanti*, Newars celebrate New Year’s Day of Nepal Sambat through *Mha Puja*, a ritual in which one’s own body is worshipped and believed to be purified and spiritually strengthened for the coming year. *Kija Puja* honours a woman’s brothers, whether or not they are related by blood. During *Sā Pāru*, people who have lost a family member in the previous year dress as cows and saints and parade through town along a specific route.

In Kathmandu, *Yenya*, or Indra Jatra, is the largest street festival. Three cars bearing the living goddess Kumari and two child gods are pulled through the streets, accompanied by masked dances. The two godchildren are Ganesh and Bhairav. During *Pahan Charhe*, portable shrines bearing images of mother goddesses are carried through Kathmandu. *Jana Baha Dyah Jatra* carries an image of Karunamaya through central Kathmandu for three days. In Lalitpur, *Bunga Dyah Jatra* continues for a month and culminates in *Bhoto Jatra*, the display of the sacred vest. *Biska Jatra*, the largest outdoor celebration in Bhaktapur, includes chariot processions and lasts nine days. *Sithi Nakha* includes worship and the cleaning of natural water sources.

## Foodways

Newar cuisine developed over centuries among Newars of the Nepal Mandala region. Food is integral to Newar culture, and dishes served during feasts and festivals have symbolic significance. Daily meals are called *Jā Neu* or *Newa Thali*, also known as *Newa Jā Bhu*. They commonly include Taichin rice, lentil soup, green vegetables, assorted vegetable dishes, meat and pickles. The morning meal is *Jyaana*, the afternoon meal *Baji*, and the evening meal *Beli*.

Rice is served as *Jā*. Other named foods include *Choila*, ground buffalo meat; *Pālulā*, buffalo meat and ginger curry; *Senlāmu*, raw ground buffalo liver seasoned with spices; *Tarkāri*, vegetable curry; *Keń*, lentil soup; *Baji*, beaten rice; *Chatānmari*, a rice-flour crepe; *Gwaramari*, deep-fried dough; *Wo* and *Bara*, fried lentil cakes; and *Kwāti*, a soup made from nine types of sprouted beans. Feast foods include *Dāyekālā*, buffalo meat curry; *Dugulā*, goat meat curry; *Heynlā*, duck curry; *Kachilā*, marinated raw minced buffalo meat; *Takhā*, jellied buffalo meat curry; *Chhoylā*, boiled or smoked buffalo meat; and *Hāku Chhoylā*, roasted, diced and marinated buffalo meat.

Festival foods include *Samaybaji*, a set of beaten rice, roasted meat, vegetables, cowpea, soybean and ginger, and *Syābaji*, parched rice. Desserts include *Dhau*, yogurt; *Juju Dhau*, yogurt or curd originating from Bhaktapur; *Laakhamari*, made from flour and sugar and cooked in hot oil; and *Yomari*, made from chaku and flour and steamed like momo. Drinks include *Aylā*, liquor; *Arak*, rice beer; *kaar-Thwon*, brown beer; and *hyāun-Thwon*, red beer. Food is eaten with bare hands, and washing the hands before and after meals is customary.

## Oral tradition & literature

Newar literature has one of the oldest literary traditions among the Tibeto-Burman languages and includes prose, poetry and drama. It began as prose in the 14th century. Early works include *Mānava Nyāyaśāstra*, a law book written in 1380, and *Gopālarāja Vaṃśāvalī*, a chronicle written in 1389. The earliest storybook in Nepal Bhasa is a translation of the *Bhagavata Purana* from 1505, commissioned by Devakidevi, daughter of King Bhuwana Malla.

Other works include *Dhon Cholecha* and *Swasthani Bakhan*. Mahendra Malla is known as Ādikavi, or first poet, of Nepal Bhasa. Newar dramas draw on epic stories, and Jagat Prakasha Malla was the first playwright in Bhaktapur to write plays in his mother tongue, Newari. The literary tradition flourished for five centuries until 1850 and later suffered decline under political oppression.

The period from 1909 to 1941 is known as the Nepal Bhasa renaissance. Writers including Nisthananda Bajracharya, Siddhidas Mahaju, Jagat Sundar Malla and Yogbir Singh Kansakar are honoured as the Four Pillars of Nepal Bhasa. The period from 1941 to 1945 is known as the jail years; Chittadhar Hridaya, Siddhicharan Shrestha and Phatte Bahadur Singh were among writers imprisoned for literary or political activities. The Nepal Bhasa movement continued through publication, education, meetings and protest rallies.

## Language & religion

Nepal Bhasa, also called Newar, belongs to the Tibeto-Burman branch of the Sino-Tibetan language family. It is predominantly spoken by Newars in Nepal’s Kathmandu Valley. Its five dialects are Kathmandu-Lalitpur, Bhaktapur, Dolakha, Chitlang and Pahari. Newar was the court and state language during the medieval period and remained a state language until 1769, after which Nepali replaced it as the national language following the Shah conquest.

The Newar script, also known as Nepal Lipi, appeared in the 10th century. Bhujimol was used from the 11th century onward and Ranjana from the 12th century onward. These scripts were used for stone and copper-plate inscriptions, coins, palm-leaf documents, and Hindu and Buddhist manuscripts.

Newars predominantly practise Newar Hinduism and Newar Buddhism. Buddhist purohits and temple priests include Gubhāju/Bajracharya, while Rajopadhyaya Brahmins serve as priests for Hindu Newars and at important shrines. Religious culture includes devotional music, ritual dance, masked dance, processions, sacred courtyards, temple worship and festivals.
